cover.artAlt: A grand stone castle with tall towers glowing warm gold at sunset, framed by a moat and green hills
cover.blurb: As the sun sets gold over the moat, this castle is full of stories waiting for you. Turn the page to cross the drawbridge and step inside.

pages.title: A Suit Made of Steel
pages.artAlt: A shining suit of knight's armour stands on display in a museum

facts.text: A full suit of battle armour usually weighed about 20 to 25 kilograms, about as heavy as a big holiday suitcase. Because the weight was spread out over the knight's whole body, it felt much lighter than it sounds.

Museum tests with real armour show that a person in a well-fitted suit could run, lie down, get up again and even climb onto a horse without any help. One famous French knight could climb the underside of a ladder using only his hands while wearing full armour.

Future knights started practising young, and boys wore armour during training so they could get used to it. The Royal Armouries museum even looks after a suit of armour made for a six-year-old boy, and two more made for brothers aged eight and ten.

pages.title: The Busiest Room in the Castle
pages.artAlt: Inside a castle's great hall, colourful banners hang above a long wooden table

facts.text: The great hall was the heart of the whole castle. The household gathered here to eat together at long tables with benches, because in a castle, mealtimes were something you shared with everyone.

Where you sat in the hall showed how important you were. The lord and the most special guests sat at the high table, placed at the end of the hall furthest from the kitchen, while everyone else sat in order down the long tables.
Castle meals were wonderfully slow. Lunch began at about 10 or 11 in the morning and could last two to three hours, with plenty of time for talking, music and second helpings.

pages.title: The Cleverest Front Door
pages.artAlt: A stone castle's drawbridge is lowered over a calm moat

facts.text: A castle entrance was a front door with moving parts. The castle's gatekeepers looked after the gate, a heavy sliding grille called a portcullis, and the drawbridge itself. With the bridge pulled up, the moat became a ring of water with no way across.

Some moats were truly enormous. At the Tower of London, workers began digging a moat right around the castle in the 1240s, and it grew to be at least 50 metres wide, which is about half a football pitch.

Moats were not just clever, they were full of life. In 1292 King Edward I sent lots of young pike to live in the Tower of London's moat as a fish farm, and archaeologists later found a centuries-old wicker fish trap there with fish skeletons still inside.

pages.title: Pictures That Say Your Name
pages.artAlt: A colourful medieval tapestry and a knight's shield hang on a stone castle wall

facts.text: When knights began wearing helmets that covered their faces, nobody could tell who was who. So each knight painted his own special mix of colours, shapes and animals on his shield and banners, a bit like writing your name in pictures.
Only one person was allowed to use each coat of arms. If you spotted a knight's design at a tournament, you knew exactly who was inside the armour, even if you could not see his face.

Tapestries were woven from wool and silk threads by craftsmen with amazing skill, and they were the great art of their day. Covering a wall with them showed visitors that the owner was someone very grand indeed.
